title: Three Ways to Span a Gap

publication.reason: Claims are source-verified, not editorially approved; no rights-cleared narration exists (silent preview).

beats.narration: Here is a gap of twenty-four metres, with a bank on each side. A bridge has to carry a deck from one bank to the other.
beats.visual_goal: Show the empty site and the span to be crossed

beats.narration: The simplest answer is a beam. In this timber bridge, beams run from one support to the next, and the deck rests on top of them.
beats.visual_goal: Introduce the timber beam bridge and its spanning members

beats.narration: Taken apart, the arrangement is easy to read: planks rest on beams, beams rest on cap beams, and cap beams sit on posts.
beats.visual_goal: Explain the beam-and-deck arrangement of the model

beats.narration: A stone arch works differently. It is built from wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs, with a keystone at the top of each arch.
beats.visual_goal: Introduce the masonry arch and show one arch ring's voussoirs and keystone

beats.narration: A truss takes another approach: many straight members joined into triangles.
beats.visual_goal: Introduce the truss and its triangulated members

beats.narration: The triangles can be arranged in different patterns. A Pratt truss has vertical members and diagonals that slope down towards the centre. A Warren truss uses alternating diagonals, with no verticals.
beats.visual_goal: Compare the Pratt and Warren web patterns on the same chords

beats.narration: Side by side, the three models span the same gap in three different ways.
beats.visual_goal: All three archetypes at identical scale on identical sites

beats.narration: Beam, arch and truss: three arrangements of parts for the same task. These are illustrations, not a timeline.
beats.visual_goal: Close on the comparison, glowing the parts that differ
